Start with what you are trying to power and for how long, not the biggest number you can afford. A 12V compressor fridge draws roughly 40-60Wh per hour of runtime (it cycles, so real draw is lower than its rated wattage), which is about 1000-1400Wh over 24 hours — within reach of a single 2kWh station if it is your only load. A residential-style AC fridge draws more, closer to 1500-2500Wh per day. A window or mini-split AC unit is the real capacity killer: even a small 5,000 BTU unit can pull 400-600W continuous, which will drain a 2kWh station in under four hours of straight running, so AC use should be treated as a generator or shore-power task, not a power-station task, unless you are running one of the very large stations built for it. For most RVers, sizing to cover lighting, device charging, a fridge, and occasional small appliances for 1-2 days without recharge — call it 1,500-2,500Wh of usable capacity — hits the sweet spot. If you want a power station to feed part of your RV's existing wiring rather than just running loose extension cords to individual appliances, you need to think about how it connects. Most portable power stations output standard NEMA 5-15 household outlets, not the 30A or 50A shore-power plugs RVs use, so you will need an adapter or a properly installed transfer switch to route power into your rig's breaker panel safely — never back-feed a panel without a transfer switch. Frequently Asked Questions Can a portable power station run my RV air conditioner? Only briefly, and only the largest stations. A small 5,000 BTU unit needs 400-600W continuous with a startup surge that can spike past 1500W, which will drain even a 2kWh station in a few hours. For sustained AC use, plan on shore power or a generator, and treat a power station as backup for everything else.
